chunks: From him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him, 'What do you say about exchanging wheat for semolina?' He said, 'Like for like, there is no objection to it.' I said to him, 'But it may have a yield (difference in quality/quantity) or there may be a surplus in it.' He said, 'It does not have a cost (of storage/maintenance).' I said, 'Yes, it does.' He said, 'This is for that (the case with cost).' He said, 'When the two items differ, there is no objection to it, two like for one like, hand to hand.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on exchanging wheat for semolina in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) elucidates the rules of *sarf* (currency/commodity exchange) by distinguishing between identical commodities, where a surplus (*ray'* or *fadl*) is permissible, and dissimilar ones, which require strict equality and immediate hand-to-hand exchange to avoid *riba*. This narration highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that the prohibition of excess applies specifically to the six ribawi items when exchanged for different types, whereas same-type exchanges allow for quality variations provided the measure is equal. The emphasis on 'hand to hand' (*yadan bi-yad*) underscores the necessity of *qabd* (possession) in the majlis of contract to prevent the speculative elements of usury.
